newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Seven pardoned as S.African amnesty deadline nears.
newsitem.headline: Seven pardoned as S.African amnesty deadline nears.

text.p: South Africa's post-apartheid "truth commission" on Thursday pardoned four anti-democracy white bombers and three anti-apartheid black vigilantes for human rights crimes in the final days of white rule.

The whites given amnesty were four right-wingers convicted of planting bombs shortly after negotiations on democracy began in 1990 between the white-led government of the day and President Nelson Mandela's then newly unbanned African National Congress.
"They walk as if the offence had never happened," Alex Boraine, deputy chairman of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, told a news conference.

He said the commission refused amnesty to nine people in prison for crimes including murder, saying some had not served recognised political groups and others had committed their crimes for personal and not for political reasons.

The announcement came a day after white former policeman Brian Mitchell was pardoned for organising an attack in which 11 blacks died in 1988 and just days before the midnight Saturday deadline for amnesty applications.
Boraine said the commission would renew its request to Mandela on Friday to extend the deadline for applications by about three months.

He said the commission also would ask Mandela to broaden the scope of the commission's work to include right-wing bombings that killed at least 21 people in the final days before the country's first all-race elections in April 1994.

Those denied pardons included Kwane Sebe, son of former apartheid homeland leader Lennox Sebe, who is in jail for attacking the homes of people judged by the commission to be personal rivals and not political enemies.
The commission's autonomous amnesty committee, headed by black judge Hassen Mall, ordered immediate release for three members of a township self-defence unit loyal to the ANC.
They were serving sentences of eight to 14 years for the murder in 1991 and 1992 of three members of a gang that terrorised their black community.

"All the applicants were members of a political party and acted against people they believed to be their political opponents. They believed...that their acts would bring an end to violence and allow freedom of political expression," the committee said in its judgment.

The committee refused amnesty to white activists Cornelius van Wyk and Jean du Plessis, whose four-member National Socialist Partisans killed two domestic workers and their white employer in a botched attempt to steal guns.
The committee said the men were bound together by their intention "of purging the country of inferior races" and were not members of a party involved in the contest over apartheid.
Boraine said the commission, which has another year to investigate the human rights record of the battle over apartheid, would accept as many applications as possible before Saturday's deadline.
"The number of applications has risen incredibly in the last week and even today. It's moving towards 4,000," he said.

Addressing objections from blacks who oppose the release of apartheid agents convicted of massacres and torture, he said: "Amnesty is the price we have had to pay for...our peaceful transition to demcoracy."
Boraine said the commission had prepared a list of questions for former president P.W. Botha, who has so far refused to testify to the commission or to seek amnesty.

"Our view is that anyone who was directly responsible and in charge of a system that brought about gross human rights violations in this country not only owes South Africa an apology, but ought, in the interests of reconciliation, to give very serious consideration to applying for amnesty," he said.
